newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi refugees speak of Zaire border killings.
newsitem.headline: Burundi refugees speak of Zaire border killings.

text.p: Burundian Hutu refugees fleeing home from eastern Zaire said on Sunday they feared that men separated from them by Burundian troops were killed in no man's land.
Aid workers said they were concerned at the reports, souring attempts to repatriate some 10,000 Burundian Hutus from the Uvira region of eastern Zaire where fighting erupted two weeks ago.
Burundian authorities supervising the repatriation deny that any soldiers were separating refugees at the border and said on Sunday the area was calm and not a shot had been fired.
"I left Uvira yesterday. When we were coming across, Burundian soldiers took some people, heads of families, away for questioning," a refugee who only gave his first name as Christopher told Reuters.
"We don't know what happened to them after that," he added. He said most of his friends survived the border crossing but he believed some of them had been killed.
Tens of thousands of Burundian and Rwandan Hutu refugees fled camps north of Uvira two weeks ago during fighting between Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels.
The Tutsi rebels, who seized both Uvira and Zaire's Rusizi plain, told Burundian Hutu refugees to go home, refugees said.
Aid workers said between 70 and 130 people were reported to have been killed in no man's land and that reports of the killings, which began circulating last Saturday, continued all week.

"We have heard Burundian authorities are doing a separation process among the men. What happens after that, who knows? If the reports are true, it is an extremely big worry," a U.N. official told Reuters.
Eight bodies including those of several children were washed ashore on Sunday at the mouth of the Rusizi River, which runs into Lake Tanganyika near Burundi's border with Zaire.
Fishermen say they have buried 50 bodies washed down the Rusizi in the last two weeks and at least 20 more are strewn along the waterfront, some partly hidden under rotting bamboo.
The face of one female corpse, her eyes bulging, arms outstretched and teeth bared, suggested a violent death. All the bodies seen by reporters on Sunday were hideously disfigured.
The Rusizi is infested with crocodiles and hippos.
"We cannot say who killed these people. The bodies started arriving here two weeks ago," a Burundian fisherman said.
But their presence, coupled with a nauseating stench from reeds near a side road running through no man's land, has alarmed aid agencies who need the cooperation of Burundian authorities.
"We cannot stick our necks out and say the army is killing people. We are just not in a position," an aid official said.
Diplomats have said the fall of Burundian Hutu refugee camps around Uvira to Tutsi rebels could give Burundi's army an upper hand in its war against Hutu rebels in the interior of the tiny country.
The rebels would no longer able to use the camps as bases for launching attacks into north and west Burundi, they add.
More than 150,000 people have been killed in three years of massacres and civil war between the Burundian army and rebels. Human rights groups accuse both sides of reprisal killings of civilians.
There are an estimated 200,000 Burundian Hutus in eastern Zaire, along with 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees and tens of thousands of Zaireans uprooted by the fighting in the last two weeks.
Zaire has accused the armies of Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of fighting alongside Tutsi rebels in its two eastern provinces of North and South Kivu. All three countries deny the charges.
But Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army sent troops into the Zairean city of Goma on Friday and Saturday after what a Rwandan officer said was a brief incursion on Tuesday over the border.
